Where it began

Munaf Patel was born on 12 July 1983 in Ikhar, in Gujarat. He was noticed unusually early. In 2003, aged 20 and with no first-class cricket behind him, Kiran More, then India's chairman of selectors, asked him to spend time at the MRF Pace Foundation in Chennai. There his speed caught the eye of Dennis Lillee, who ran the place, and of Steve Waugh, who was visiting.

With Sachin Tendulkar's support he joined Mumbai late in 2003, without having played a game for Gujarat. He later moved on to Maharashtra, in 2005, and over the years he also turned out for West Zone in the Duleep Trophy.

The player

His chance came after he took 10 wickets for the Board President's XI against the touring England side. Picked for the second Test, at Mohali, he took 7 for 97 in the match, including 4 for 25 in the second innings, and he moved the ball both ways.

He played 13 Tests for India from 2006 to 2011 and took 35 wickets at 38.54, with that debut 4 for 25 as his best. One-day cricket brought him some of his happiest days. He was man of the match against England at the 2006 Champions Trophy with 3 for 18. Before the 2011 World Cup he took 4 for 29 in South Africa as India defended 190 and won by a single run. At the World Cup itself he took four wickets against Bangladesh, held a return catch to remove Kevin Pietersen in the tie with England, and played in both the semi-final against Pakistan, back at Mohali, and the final. He finished a World Cup winner.

What made him special

He was quick, often above 85 miles per hour and sometimes beyond 90, but what impressed people most was his control. Pace and accuracy together are a rare pairing, and he had both.

With the bat he was happy to leave things to others. He made 60 Test runs, with a top score of 15 not out, which is a fair sign of where his talents lay.

Away from the middle

He did well in the Indian Premier League. He took 14 wickets for Rajasthan Royals in the very first season, when they won the title, and in 2011 he had his best year, 22 wickets for Mumbai Indians, including 5 for 21 against Kings XI Punjab at Mohali.

He retired in November 2018 and turned to coaching. In 2025 he was bowling coach for Delhi Capitals in the IPL, and that same year he took the same role with Seattle Orcas in Major League Cricket.

And finally

Mohali seems to have been kind to him. It was where he began his Test career, where he took 5 for 21 in the IPL and where he helped India into a World Cup final. Most bowlers would settle for one happy ground. He found one that kept giving.
